basis: division tears the community as Christ's body
note: Clement condemns strife as tearing apart members of one body; this makes communal loss the consequence of the division the commentary seeks to overcome.
The commentary traces damage from disputes among believers; Clement asks why strife, anger, divisions and war appear among the community, confronting its internal fracture.

basis: love acts in harmony and creates no schism
note: Clement describes love as refusing division and doing everything in harmony; this is a Christian interpretive expansion of the bond that the commentary sees replacing estrangement.

basis: one person gives way so the community may live in peace
note: Clement asks anyone causing strife to leave voluntarily if needed so the flock can live peacefully; this gives the commentary's peace a costly communal practice.

basis: reconcile with an opponent before the communal meal
note: The Didache bars someone at odds with a fellow from joining the Eucharist until reconciliation; this gives the commentary's peace a concrete liturgical consequence.
The commentary repairs ties among believers; the Didache bars a person with a dispute from joining the assembly until reconciled, making peace a condition of its common offering.
The commentary turns adversarial truth claims into mutual counsel; the Didache directs communal reproof without anger and in peace, joining correction to a nonhostile manner.

basis: correct rather than hate a person
note: The commentary's counsel must be joined to affection; the Didache forbids hatred and distinguishes those one should correct, pray for, or love beyond oneself.

basis: reconcile disputants, judge rightly, reprove without partiality
note: The teaching rejects division, orders reconciliation and fair judgment, then forbids partiality in reproof; it closely joins the commentary's peace, haqq, and mutual counsel.

basis: make peace between those who quarrel
note: The commentary moves from arguing parties to active reconciliation; the Didache forbids causing division and directs its reader to make peace among people in dispute.

basis: share with a brother in need
note: The commentary's fellowship reaches the needy rather than merely speaking to them; the Didache tells its reader to share possessions with a brother and not claim them as exclusively one's own.

basis: love and guard the brother as one's own soul
note: The saying treats the brother's life as one's own to protect; it gives the commentary's close-friend image an unusually intimate ethical measure.
The commentary turns reciprocal contention into joined counsel; Paul urges the community to agree in speech and be restored to one mind without divisions.
The commentary begins with a community at odds; Paul reports quarrels among the Corinthian brothers, the precise communal fracture addressed by his appeal to unity.

basis: one hungry while another is full
note: The commentary cites failure to urge food for the needy; in the Corinthians' common meal, one goes hungry while another becomes drunk, exposing a failed shared table.
The commentary's failed urging to feed the poor has communal consequences; Paul rebukes the Corinthians for shaming members who have nothing at their shared meal.

basis: wait for one another at the meal
note: The commentary's reciprocity must include material care; Paul tells the gathered Corinthians to wait for one another when they eat, answering the hungry member's exclusion in the same scene.
Paul's body image rejects division and makes members care for one another; it pictures mutual attachment as protection against isolation.

basis: members care for each other without division
note: The commentary's reciprocal ethic overcomes separated parties; Paul's body image says members should have the same care for one another so the body has no division.

basis: one member's suffering is shared by all
note: The body's members suffer and rejoice together; this turns the commentary's human-in-loss image into shared rather than solitary experience.
The commentary's one-sided isolation becomes shared life; Paul's members suffer or rejoice together as each member is affected.
Paul makes patience and kindness qualities of love between people; this gives the commentary's ṣabr a relational rather than solitary form.
The commentary's affectionate bond is maintained by sabr; Paul's description of love begins with patience and kindness, placing endurance inside interpersonal love.
Paul joins truth with love's response; this directly meets the commentary's shift from haqq as a contested claim to a shared good.
The commentary binds love to mutual transmission of haqq; Paul says love does not rejoice in wrongdoing but rejoices with truth.
The commentary's companion stays with the community in patience; Paul's love bears and endures all things, giving that steadfastness a relational subject.
The commentary starts with rival claims inside a group; Paul points to jealousy and strife among the Corinthians as evidence of immature, merely human behavior.
The commentary's rival claims need someone to reconcile or judge them; Paul asks whether no wise person in the community can decide a matter between brothers.
The commentary's first scene is two sides disputing right despite their possible bond; Paul names the scandal of a brother bringing a brother to court before unbelievers.

basis: accepting wrong instead of litigating with a brother
note: The commentary turns haqq into truth passed mutually, while Paul says that lawsuits among believers are already defeat and asks why they do not accept being wronged; the differing remedy is the point.
The commentary's human being is in loss until a shared ethic replaces contention; Paul calls lawsuits among believers already a defeat and asks why they do not bear wrong.
The commentary's claimed right can become injury to the other side; Paul says the litigating Corinthians themselves wrong and defraud their own brothers, reversing the ethic of mutual benefit.

basis: walking in light yields fellowship with one another
note: The letter joins shared truthfulness before God to fellowship among believers; this connects the commentary's haqq with its movement toward closeness.

basis: love of brothers and escape from death
note: The commentary contrasts the human in loss with believers joined by affection; John says love for brothers marks a passage from death to life.
The commentary's close friendship issues in righteous action; John says Christ's laying down his life teaches believers to lay down their lives for brothers.
The commentary invokes the failure to encourage food for the poor; John asks how God's love can remain in one who sees a needy brother and shuts up compassion.
The commentary's joined good deeds and shared haqq require action; John tells the community to love in deed and truth, not merely in speech.

basis: claiming love for God while hating a brother is false
note: The letter tests religious claim against treatment of the visible brother; this challenges any haqq claim detached from mutual care.
The commentary insists on concrete closeness between believers; John calls one who claims to love God while hating a visible brother a liar.

basis: love of God entails love of brother
note: The commentary binds faith to affection among companions; John says the command received from God is that the one loving God must also love his brother.
The letter commands active pursuit of peace, matching the commentary's account of peace as removing recoil and separation.
The commentary makes peace an action beyond ceasing a dispute; Peter tells readers to turn from evil, do good, and seek and pursue peace.

basis: unity, sympathy, brotherly love, and humility
note: Peter places one-mindedness and brotherly compassion together; this gives the commentary's move from estrangement to intimacy a compact communal ethic.
The commentary develops closeness from estrangement; Peter asks all to have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love and humility.
The commentary's enemy-to-friend turn requires patience; Peter forbids returning evil or reviling in kind and commands blessing instead.
Peter says sustained love covers many sins; this fits the commentary's transition from contention toward a bond that can absorb offense.
The commentary's patience permits estranged companions to stay together; Peter urges sustained love for one another because love covers a multitude of sins.
The commentary's reciprocal care keeps others close; Peter asks members to show hospitality to one another without complaint, giving affectionate attachment a household practice.
The commentary's mutual action makes the community stronger; Paul tells believers to encourage and build one another, noting that they already do so.

basis: admonish, encourage, help, and be patient with all
note: The community is to give different forms of support to the idle, fainthearted, and weak, then remain patient with everyone; this is reciprocal counsel enacted as care.
The commentary's companion stands with others in patience; Paul assigns differentiated mutual duties to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak and be patient with all.
The commentary's mutual action replaces retaliation; Paul forbids repaying evil for evil and directs believers always to seek good for one another and everyone.

basis: restore, encourage, agree, and live in peace
note: Paul joins restoration and mutual encouragement to agreement and peace, closely matching the commentary's sequence from conflict to togetherness.
The commentary's peace removes fearful estrangement; Paul urges the community to forgive and comfort a punished person so excessive sorrow does not overwhelm him.
The commentary turns disagreement toward an enduring bond; Paul asks the community to confirm its love for the person it disciplined, making affection an explicit act of restoration.
The commentary transforms the opponent into a companion through counsel; Paul says the disobedient member is to be admonished as a brother rather than regarded as an enemy.
The commentary's opening rivals fight over what they call right; this instruction says foolish and ignorant controversies produce quarrels, supplying a diagnosis of failed counsel.

basis: the Lord's servant must not quarrel but be patient
note: The teacher is to avoid strife, remain gentle, and endure patiently; this directly links sabr to how one handles opponents.
The commentary reverses rival claims into patient counsel; this instruction says the Lord's servant must not quarrel but be kind to everyone and able to teach.
Correction is to be offered gently even to those who oppose; this gives mutual counsel a manner aimed at restoration rather than victory.
The commentary's truth is conveyed to the other side instead of used for contention; the servant corrects opponents with gentleness in hope of their turning toward truth.
The believers' serious dispute over Gentile inclusion gives the commentary's contested claims a concrete communal case rather than a generic quarrel.

basis: communal decision reached with the Spirit and the assembly
note: The council says its decision seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them together; this gives the preceding dispute a shared, non-solitary resolution.

The commentary moves contention toward companionship; Paul and Barnabas instead have a sharp disagreement and separate, showing that fellow believers' dispute can remain unresolved in the narrated moment.

basis: one heart and soul with possessions shared
note: The believers hold themselves as one community and treat possessions as common; this gives the commentary's people-joining image a material practice.
The commentary moves from the lone human to a mutually sustaining believing group; Acts depicts the multitude of believers as one heart and soul, with no private claim to possessions.
The commentary cites neglect of the needy as failure of shared obligation; Acts reports a complaint of Hellenists against Hebrews because their widows were overlooked in daily distribution.

basis: Barnabas introduces feared Saul to the apostles
note: When the disciples fear Saul, Barnabas stands with him and vouches for his changed life; an intermediary turns aversion into acceptance.

basis: bear with and forgive one another
note: The instruction makes forbearance and forgiveness reciprocal; it shows patience operating directly between people.
The commentary's sabr supports reconciliation where people have complaints; Paul tells believers to bear with and forgive one another when a complaint arises.
Love is named the bond that brings the virtues to completion; this adds a binding image to the commentary's account of people joining one another.
The commentary names affection and kinship as a bond whose absence marks distance; Paul calls love the bond that completes the virtues.

basis: peace of Christ rules in one body
note: The one body is to be governed by peace; this links reconciliation with the communal unity developed in the commentary.
The commentary's separated people become a connected believing group; Paul says Christ's peace should rule in their hearts because they were called in one body.
The commentary's repeated reciprocal verb makes each a giver and receiver of counsel; Paul says the word should dwell richly in the community as members teach and admonish one another.

basis: Christ makes two groups one by breaking hostility
note: The letter pictures peace as removing the dividing wall between groups; this gives the commentary's sulh a concrete image of estrangement dismantled.
The commentary depicts enemies becoming close; Christ makes two groups one and breaks their dividing wall of hostility, an explicit transformation of social distance.
The commentary's hostile sides become a joined group; Paul describes reconciling both groups to God in one body through the cross and killing the hostility.

basis: truth spoken in love grows the body
note: The letter links truth-telling to love and the growth of the whole body; this adds a communal result to the commentary's exchange of haqq.
The commentary's haqq is shared within recovered affection; speaking truth in love builds growth into Christ, making the manner of transmission part of the truth's work.

basis: patience bears with one another in love
note: The community is told to practice humility, patience, and forbearance toward one another; this connects the commentary's ṣabr to sustaining relationship.

basis: patience bearing one another in love
note: The commentary links patience to standing beside a companion; Paul joins patience, humility and bearing with one another in love as the practice of shared life.

basis: speak truth to neighbor because members belong to one another
note: Paul joins truthful speech to mutual membership in one body; this directly links the commentary's haqq with its hand-to-hand relation.

basis: truth to neighbor because members of each other
note: The commentary insists each participant gives and receives truth; Paul commands truthful speech to one's neighbor because believers are members of one another.

basis: speech that builds the other up
note: The commentary's mutual exhortation gives another person what is needed; Paul asks for speech suited to building up hearers and giving them grace, rather than harmful talk.

basis: unity held by the bond of peace
note: The letter describes peace as the bond that preserves communal unity; this closely meets the commentary's movement from aversion to attachment.
The commentary's separated people are joined again; Paul asks believers to maintain the Spirit's unity in the bond of peace, turning attachment into a sustained task.
The commentary says peace removes estrangement; Paul asks members to be kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another as God forgave them.
The commentary says peace removes frightened separation; Peter withdraws from eating with Gentiles because he fears the circumcision group, a concrete reverse of shared company.
The commentary turns contest over haqq into truth shared for the community's good; Paul challenges Peter's withdrawal publicly because it contradicts the truth of the gospel.
The commentary changes mutual action from dispute into affectionate service; Paul commands believers to use freedom to serve one another through love.
The commentary says contention weakens a community; Paul warns that biting and devouring one another can end with the disputants consumed by each other.
Paul says to restore a caught person in a spirit of gentleness while watching oneself; correction becomes mutual care rather than adversarial judgment.
The commentary makes counsel a patient act for a companion's good; Paul directs spiritual members to restore someone caught in a transgression gently while watching their own vulnerability.
The command to carry one another's burdens makes the commentary's move from the solitary human to companions who stand together concrete.
The commentary's members give and receive aid; Paul tells them to bear each other's burdens, turning companionship into a concrete shared action.

basis: consider one another and stir up love and good works
note: The letter makes attention to others the source of mutual encouragement toward good deeds, closely joining the commentary's work and reciprocal advice.

basis: spur one another to love and good works
note: The commentary joins mutual urging to righteous deeds and affection; Hebrews asks believers to consider how to stir each other toward love and good works.

basis: encourage one another as the day approaches
note: The command to encourage each other makes perseverance communal, matching the commentary's counsel of patience passed between people.
The commentary joins companions who might separate; Hebrews contrasts neglect of meeting together with mutual encouragement as the day approaches.
The commentary presents peace as an active repair of alienation; Hebrews commands pursuing peace with all, alongside holiness.
The commentary's link between people can be broken by a growing quarrel; Hebrews warns that a bitter root can spring up, cause trouble and defile many.
The commentary highlights mutual exhortation as the way out of loss; Hebrews commands daily mutual exhortation so no one is hardened by deceitful sin.
The commentary's reciprocal counsel requires receiving the other's word and patient speech; James commands quick hearing, slow speaking and slow anger.

basis: brother or sister lacks food and clothes
note: The commentary cites failure to urge food for the poor as a breach of mutual obligation; James places a needy brother or sister without daily food before the speaking community.

basis: go in peace without giving food
note: The commentary insists on good deeds beside faith and on real care for the needy; James depicts someone wishing a needy person peace but withholding bodily necessities, exposing empty peaceful speech.
The commentary cites quarrel as loss of collective strength; James says jealousy and selfish ambition bring disorder and every vile practice.
The commentary's truth is passed without quarrel; James describes wisdom from above as peaceable, gentle and open to reason, an ethical mode for exchanging counsel.

basis: righteousness is sown in peace by peacemakers
note: James makes peace the soil and peacemakers the agents of a harvest of righteousness; this directly joins the commentary's haqq and sulh.
The commentary joins righteous works to the ending of quarrel; James says a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by peacemakers.
The commentary begins with two sides contesting right; James asks where their wars and fights come from and locates them in desires at war within them.

basis: confess and pray for one another
note: The commentary's reciprocal counsel includes receiving help; James commands mutual confession and prayer so members may be healed, joining truthful disclosure to reciprocal care.

basis: turn a person wandering from truth
note: The commentary's counsel is something believers do for one another; James envisages one member bringing back another who has wandered from the truth.
The commentary's mutual counsel averts loss; James says turning a sinner back from error saves that person's soul from death.
The commentary's members advise and sustain each other in affection; Jesus commands disciples to love one another as he has loved them.
The commentary's reciprocal bond defines the believing group; Jesus says others will recognize his disciples by their love for one another.

basis: Jesus calls disciples friends and shares what he heard
note: The disciples are friends because Jesus has made known what he heard; this connects the commentary's intimate friend with counsel and disclosure.
The commentary's intimate friend receives truth rather than being held at a distance; Jesus calls disciples friends because he has made known to them what he heard from his Father.
The commentary's stranger or enemy can become a caring companion; the Samaritan responds with compassion to an injured traveler, crossing a socially fraught boundary.
The commentary cites mercy and the failure to encourage care for the needy; the Samaritan binds the traveler's wounds and takes him to shelter, embodying practical care.
The commentary moves from distance to close relation; Jesus' interlocutor identifies the neighbor as the one who showed mercy, making companionship an action rather than prior kinship.
Jesus commands attention to a brother's wrongdoing; with the following forgiveness instruction, correction serves the relationship rather than a contest over right.
The commentary joins truthful counsel with repaired kinship; Jesus directs a disciple to rebuke a sinning brother and forgive him on repentance, giving both actions their place.
Jesus says to forgive the same brother even after repeated offenses if he repents; this makes patience a repeated practice sustaining kinship.

basis: be at peace with one another after rivalry
note: After the disciples argue over greatness and dispute who belongs with them, Jesus tells them to have salt and be at peace with one another; the instruction answers internal rivalry directly.

basis: be at peace with one another
note: The commentary ends with reciprocal action among believers; Jesus explicitly tells his disciples to have peace with one another after their dispute about rank.
The commentary cites quarrelling as the cause of a group's weakened force; Jesus says a kingdom divided against itself is laid waste and a divided city or house will not stand.

basis: private correction aims to regain a brother
note: The offended person is to speak directly and, if heard, has gained a brother; this makes admonition a means of restoring kinship rather than winning a case.
The commentary makes truth something passed to the other person rather than fought over; Jesus tells one to confront a sinning brother privately with the aim of gaining him.
The commentary's reciprocal action draws separated members into concord; Jesus says two who agree on earth about a request will be heard by the Father, within his teaching on community disputes.
The commentary's togetherness must survive renewed wrongs; Peter asks how often to forgive a brother who sins against him, identifying a concrete strain on kinship.
Jesus tells Peter to forgive not a few times but repeatedly; this extends the commentary's patience into sustained repair after recurring offense.
The commentary's patience sustains restored ties; Jesus' answer to Peter rejects a small limit on forgiving a brother, extending reconciliation beyond a single settlement.
The commentary's peace must heal the bond beneath formal settlement; Jesus closes the unforgiving servant story by requiring forgiveness of one's brother from the heart.
The commentary says human bonds must be put right; Jesus makes the brother's grievance significant even at the altar, supplying the circumstance for the reconciliation commanded next.

basis: reconcile with a brother before offering a gift
note: Jesus makes repair with an estranged brother prior to altar worship; the scene gives social reconciliation priority over a religious act.
The commentary's fractured bond must be repaired; Jesus instructs a worshiper to first reconcile with a brother who has a grievance, making restored relation prior to the offering.

basis: settle quickly with an accuser on the way to court
note: The instruction to reach agreement with one's legal opponent before judgment directly meets the commentary's opening image of parties asserting their own right.
The commentary's opening parties contest a right; Jesus urges agreement with an accuser while still on the way, providing a concrete settlement before judgment escalates the quarrel.
The commentary's hostility is reversed toward intimacy; Jesus directs love and prayer toward enemies and persecutors, making the change an active response to opponents.
The commentary says peace removes human estrangement; Jesus calls peacemakers blessed and children of God, assigning positive standing to the reconciling action.

basis: correct yourself before correcting your brother
note: Jesus requires removing one's own plank before helping a brother with his speck; this checks mutual claims of right with self-examination before advice.
The commentary calls for righteous action joined to mutual counsel; Paul directs the community to do everything without grumbling or disputes.
The commentary's separate claimants become an affectionate company; Paul asks the Philippians to be of one mind and the same love.
Paul's instruction to count others above oneself counters each party's insistence that haqq belongs to it, though it frames humility rather than mutual truth-telling.

basis: Euodia and Syntyche urged to agree in the Lord
note: Paul names two women who labored in the gospel and asks them to reach agreement; the personal appeal makes counsel address an actual community conflict.
The commentary develops a specific transition from contention to togetherness; Paul appeals to Euodia and Syntyche by name to have the same mind in the Lord.

basis: a companion asked to help the women reconcile
note: Paul asks a trusted coworker to assist the women who struggled beside him; the continuation makes reconciliation a shared responsibility.
The commentary's close companion stands by members of the group; Paul asks a true companion to help the two women who worked beside him in the gospel.
The commentary traces a move from frightened distance to enduring attachment; Paul suggests Onesimus was separated from Philemon for a time so Philemon might have him back forever.

basis: receive Onesimus as a beloved brother
note: Paul asks Philemon to receive the formerly enslaved Onesimus no longer merely as a slave but as a beloved brother; the appeal turns hierarchy and estrangement toward kinship.

basis: receive a slave as beloved brother
note: The commentary's distant parties become family; Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer merely as a slave but as a beloved brother.

basis: mutual affection and honoring one another
note: Paul commands familial affection and outdoing one another in honor; this is a direct ethic of reciprocal closeness.
The commentary develops the close friend's affection and reciprocal giving; Paul commands brotherly love and outdoing one another in showing honor.

basis: live peaceably with everyone as far as possible
note: Paul makes peace an active communal aim while acknowledging limits; this fits the commentary's removal of estrangement without specifying a single dispute.
The commentary places responsibility on each party to end contention; Paul instructs believers, so far as it depends on them, to live peaceably with everyone.

basis: feed and give drink to an enemy
note: Paul prescribes care for an enemy in need; this is a concrete act by which the commentary's enemy-to-close-friend movement can begin.
The commentary cites both enemy-to-friend reversal and urging care for the poor; Paul commands feeding and giving drink to an enemy in need, locating the reversal in an act of mercy.
Paul's concluding principle explains how good action can change the relation to an enemy, adding an ethical mechanism to the commentary's transformation.
The commentary's enemies become friends through patiently choosing another response; Paul commands overcoming evil with good instead of being overcome by it.

basis: welcome the dissenter without quarrelling over opinions
note: Paul instructs the community to receive the person with a different food practice without turning opinions into a fight; this answers the commentary's move from claims to belonging.
Paul joins the pursuit of peace to building one another up; this closely matches the commentary's reciprocal movement from contested truth to mutual counsel.
The commentary makes each believer responsible for another's progress; Paul calls them to pursue what makes for peace and builds one another up amid disputes over conduct.

basis: eater and abstainer must not despise or judge
note: Paul names both sides of the practice dispute and says God has welcomed each; this directly checks mutual claims of moral superiority.
The commentary stresses that each person both gives and receives counsel; Paul says the Romans are full of goodness and knowledge and able to admonish one another.

basis: welcome one another as Christ welcomed you
note: The community's welcome is grounded in the welcome it has received; this makes inclusion reciprocal rather than a claim held by one side.
The commentary's estranged parties become companions; Paul commands mutual welcome as Christ has welcomed them, giving the bond a concrete reception practice.

basis: warn then separate from divisive person
note: The commentary emphasizes holding a group together through counsel; Titus directs warning a divisive person twice and then having nothing further to do with him, marking a limit to maintained companionship.
The commentary's reconciliation changes how people address one another; Titus orders believers to avoid quarrels and show gentleness to all people.

basis: Aaron reconciles two disputants through personal messages
note: The tradition depicts Aaron telling each disputant that the other regrets the quarrel until they meet and embrace; it turns the commentary's mutual counsel into a specific practice of restoring bonds.
The commentary's two disputants need an action that reconnects them; this elaboration of Aaron as peacemaker depicts him approaching each estranged party to bring about reunion.

basis: Jerusalem destroyed for insisting on strict law
note: The Talmud interprets the city's destruction as a failure to go beyond the letter of law; this provides a Jewish counter-reading in which claiming formal right without generosity cannot sustain peace.

The commentary's reciprocal truth requires a giver and receiver; Rabbi Yohanan mourns Resh Lakish's challenging objections because their exchange developed the teaching, unlike a companion who only confirms him.

basis: scholars increase peace in the world
note: The Talmud reads the scriptural promise of peace through the work of scholars; this links the commentary's mutual counsel to peace-making, though by an interpretive bridge.

basis: Hillel's school presents Shammai's view before its own
note: The schools' dispute remains a shared search, and Hillel's humility and fair teaching explain why his view prevails; this gives the commentary's opposing claims a model of argument that preserves relationship.
The commentary's reciprocal truth requires receiving as well as giving; the houses dispute law, but Hillel's house wins praise for humility and teaching Shammai's view before its own.

The commentary's two sides can transmit truth and still become companions; this interpretation pictures father and son or teacher and pupil contending fiercely in Torah study yet parting as loving friends.

The commentary's rivals both assert right, yet peace changes the result; the rabbinic reading of judgment of peace in Zechariah 8:16 identifies compromise as a way to join adjudication and reconciliation.

basis: bringing peace between a person and a fellow
note: The Talmud names interpersonal peacemaking among deeds rewarded in this world; this gives the commentary's sulh a concrete ethical practice.
The commentary treats reconciliation as work among opposed people; the rabbinic list of deeds whose benefits extend into the world to come includes making peace between one person and another.

basis: the neighbor treated by the golden rule
note: Hillel summarizes Torah through the instruction not to do to another what one hates; this makes mutual regard the test for how one treats a fellow.
The dictum that all Israel are guarantors for one another states the mutual obligation implicit when the commentary says each gives and receives counsel.

basis: jesters cheer the sad and reconcile quarrelers
note: The two men describe both lifting the downcast and making peace between disputants; their paired actions join companionship in loss to active reconciliation.
The commentary contrasts the human alone in loss with the belonging of companions; the Honi story ends with a scholar unable to find companions and a saying that one needs fellowship or death.

basis: Hillel and Shammai preserve marriages despite legal disagreement
note: The schools disagree about rulings yet do not refuse intermarriage; this shows opposing claims coexisting without severing kinship.
The commentary's parties can disagree yet preserve kinship; the houses of Shammai and Hillel did not refrain from marrying one another despite their disputes.
The commentary binds haqq and sulh together; the rabbinic permission to change words for peace presses the question of how truthful speech serves a repaired relationship.

basis: baseless hatred brings the Second Temple's destruction
note: The Talmud explains a communal catastrophe through hatred among people; this makes estrangement itself a source of collective loss.

basis: Truth and Peace contest creating humanity
note: The commentary's human being is threatened by contention while truth and peace must be joined; this midrash personifies Truth and Peace as disputing whether humanity should be created, because humans lie and quarrel.

basis: Aaron loves peace and brings people near Torah
note: The Mishnah interprets peacemaking as active pursuit joined to love of people and drawing them near; it expands the commentary's sulh from ending repulsion to restoring closeness.

The commentary treats peace as ending estrangement and drawing people into closeness; Hillel's maxim to be Aaron's disciple joins loving and pursuing peace with loving people and drawing them near Torah.

basis: if only for myself, what am I
note: The commentary's solitary human cannot escape loss through self-concern; Hillel's question makes the inadequacy of living only for oneself explicit.

basis: justice, truth, and peace sustain the world
note: The Mishnah places justice, truth, and peace together as the world's supports; this gives a compact ethical frame for the commentary's claims of haqq, peace, and communal relation.

basis: stay with the community; do not judge before knowing one's place
note: The Mishnah warns against separation from the community and premature judgment of another; this answers the commentary's isolated human and the disputants each sure of their own right.
The commentary contrasts the solitary human with a believing company; Hillel's instruction not to separate oneself from the community treats continued belonging as a deliberate duty.

basis: divine presence rests where two discuss Torah
note: The Mishnah makes shared study a sacred meeting between people; it gives the commentary's reciprocal counsel a setting in which relationship itself matters.

basis: wisdom comes from learning from every person
note: Ben Zoma defines the wise person as one who learns from everyone; this makes the commentary's reciprocal relation a source of wisdom rather than solitary possession.

The Mishnah contrasts enduring disputes for Heaven, exemplified by Hillel and Shammai, with a dispute that does not endure; it distinguishes principled disagreement from contention that destroys bonds.

The commentary initially places claim against claim, then makes truth serve the bond; this maxim distinguishes principled Hillel-Shammai disagreement from Korah's dispute, qualifying any simple condemnation of disagreement.

basis: peace between people as a deed with lasting fruit
note: The Mishnah explicitly lists making peace between one person and another among deeds whose fruit is enjoyed in this world; it links the commentary's good action to repaired relations.

basis: one human ancestor taught as a basis for peace among creatures
note: The Mishnah says humanity descends from one person so no one can claim a superior ancestry; this directly counters rival claims and grounds common human dignity in kinship.

basis: neighbor-love as a great principle of Torah
note: Rabbi Akiva reads love of one's neighbor as a great principle; this interpretation makes the commentary's intimacy and mutual care a frame for the wider law.

basis: forgive a neighbor before praying for forgiveness
note: Ben Sira makes forgiveness of another the condition mirrored in one's own prayer; this gives the commentary's repair of hostility a reciprocal religious practice.
The commentary's rival claims need the grievance to end so the bond can resume; Sirach commands forgiveness of a neighbor's wrong and connects that act with receiving pardon in prayer.

basis: avoid strife because anger kindles it
note: The sage says restraint from quarrel reduces sin and a hot-tempered person ignites conflict; this closely joins patience with the prevention of strife.

basis: a faithful friend is a sturdy shelter and a treasure
note: Ben Sira gives the close friend a protective role; this concretizes the commentary's intimate bond as refuge in human vulnerability.
The commentary's close friend gives security after frightened separation; Sirach calls a faithful friend a sturdy shelter and a treasure, making companionship protective.

basis: a faithful friend is life-saving medicine
note: The friend is described as healing support found by those who fear God; this adds the companion's restorative effect to the commentary's account of connection.

basis: peaceful speech to someone who sinned
note: The commentary's counsel repairs a bond after wrongdoing; this testament urges love among brothers and peaceful speech to someone who sins against a companion. The exact verse division within chapter 6 is uncertain from memory.

basis: rejected counsel ends in the people's division
note: After Rehoboam rejects the elders' advice, Israel refuses his rule and separates; this shows the social loss that follows counsel answered with hardness.

basis: elders advise the king to serve and answer gently
note: The elders tell Rehoboam that serving the people and speaking good words will win their service; this makes reciprocal regard a practical alternative to coercive rule.
The commentary names affection and kinship as bonds among close friends; Jonathan's soul is knit to David's and he loves David as himself, giving narrative form to chosen attachment.
The commentary's close companions remain connected through difficulty; Jonathan sends David away in peace under a covenant binding them and their descendants.

basis: Abigail's counsel keeps David from bloodguilt
note: David blesses Abigail for restraining him from revenge; her wise intervention makes counsel the means by which a violent conflict is prevented.

basis: captives treated as kin and returned
